lines: Notice that none of these three things look like the same kind of problem at first glance.
A missing comment, a comment that shows back up, a reply sitting above the thing it's replying to.
One store produced all three, and by the end of this topic you'll be able to name exactly which guarantee each one breaks.
Before you pick, think about what the store is promising just by staying available through a partition.
Something has to give. The question is how much.
answer: Causal, and the reasoning has nothing to do with causal being a nice compromise.
Sequential consistency and linearizability both require a node to stop answering during a partition if it can't be sure of the order.
A store that refuses to ever stop answering has already ruled those two out, no matter which anomalies it would like to avoid.

lines: Hold onto what's still required here, because it's easy to assume this model gives everything up.
Every operation still lands in one shared order, and each process's own operations still show up in that order the way it issued them.
What's gone is any promise that the order tracks the clock on the wall.
Watch what actually creates the ordering requirement in this example, because it isn't time.
Barbarella's answer depends on having read the question first. That dependency is what ties her reply to the question, not when her reply happened to arrive.
Her answer and Cyrus's answer depend on nothing of each other, so nothing forces them into one shared order anywhere.
This result is worth slowing down for, because the two conditions attached to it are doing real work.
Always available, and one-way convergent. Drop either one and a stronger model becomes reachable again.
What's being claimed is narrow and precise: among stores that make both of those promises, nothing beats this one.
Go through these one at a time, because treating them as a bundle hides how independent they are.

Your own next read seeing your own last write. Your reads never sliding backward. Your writes landing everywhere in the order you made them. A write you make after a read never appearing to have happened before that read.
Each of those can fail while the other three hold perfectly, which is exactly why a store has to be checked against all four separately.
Map the hook back onto what you just learned, because both anomalies have exact names now.
The vanishing comment is a broken read-your-writes. The reply ahead of its comment is a broken writes-follow-reads.
What this topic won't do is tell you those four guarantees, added together, equal causal consistency. That claim needs more reading than got done here, so it stays unclaimed.
Carry forward the shape of the ladder, not just two names on it.
Sequential consistency keeps one order and drops the clock. Causal consistency keeps almost nothing except cause and effect, and it's the proven ceiling once a store refuses to ever stop answering.
Four session guarantees sit underneath both, each one a separate, checkable promise about a single client's own session.
Before you answer, notice exactly whose behavior each of those two guarantees is actually about.
Both of them describe what one client sees of its own past operations, nothing about what a different client sees.
answer: No, and the gap is exactly the chat example from earlier in this topic.
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads both stay inside one client's own session.
Causal consistency has to reach across clients. Nothing in those two guarantees says what Barbarella sees of Attiya's question at all.
